summary:
Article 319 of Senegal's 1965 Penal Code criminalises an "improper or unnatural act" with a person of the same sex. The penalty is one to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 1,500,000 CFA francs, and the maximum is applied whenever the act is committed with a person under 21. The provision is drafted around the sex of the participants; it makes no reference to transgender status, gender identity or gender expression.

An amendment adopted in 2026 raises that penalty to five to ten years and fines of 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs. The bill was presented on 25 February 2026, adopted on 12 March, signed on 30 March and published on 31 March. It adds an explicit ban on the promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, together with a penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith. The government's draft, adopted in February 2026, raised the maximum fine from 1.5 million to 10 million CFA francs and targeted organisations promoting what it called LGBT philosophy through film, television or writing.

The promotion and support ban is the provision that reaches trans expression directly. It criminalises advocacy and funding for transsexuality rather than sexual conduct alone, so a visitor who speaks publicly, organises, or gives money to trans-related activity is exposed under the same article as the conduct offence.

Enforcement is documented. In September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos of them circulated; the detentions formed part of a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections. In February 2026, 22 gay men were arrested within two weeks, among them a man detained on 20 February at the Senegal-Gambian border while attempting to leave the country. A separate report counted 17 arrests for "acts against nature" in early February 2026. In August, 99 men were arrested; 28 were released and 71 faced up to 20 years after the maximum was doubled.

Police practice compounds the statutory risk. Arrests have been made on second-hand reports alone, and detainees have been badly treated in custody because of their sexual orientation. Two women detained in January after a kissing video circulated were released on bail without formal charge. In October, a Dakar court sentenced one man to four years and a 200,000 CFA franc fine for acts against nature plus arms and battery, and a second man to three years.

An earlier prosecution shows how far the process can run before it collapses. Nine men were arrested on 19 December 2008 in a Dakar flat and convicted on 6 January 2009 to five years for indecent conduct and unnatural acts, plus three years for membership of a criminal group. They were tortured repeatedly in police custody and held segregated because other inmates threatened them. The convictions were overturned in April 2009 and all nine were released immediately.

Senegal has no legal gender recognition procedure. No law broadly protects LGBTQ people from discrimination; the only related provisions are limited restrictions on revealing or stigmatising depiction of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as gender-nonconforming or gay is documented. On 28 October 2023 the body of Cheikh Fall, a 31-year-old man buried in Léona Niassene cemetery, was dug up and burned in the street in Kaolack after it was revealed he was gay; four men were arrested on 30 October, while images from the scene showed a crowd of hundreds around the fire. In December 2012 a gay male couple near Dakar were beaten by a parent after being caught having sex. In May 2009 the corpse of a person locally described as goor-gigen, man-woman, was disinterred twice in Thies, left beside the grave and then dumped outside the family home after reburial.

Transgender people, counted within the LGBT population, face criminal prosecution, arrest, widespread discrimination, social intolerance and violence. Local organisations keep an exceedingly low profile because of the criminal provisions and the stigma, and the media rarely report hatred or violence directed at them.

Hostility extends to speech about the subject. A political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for giving a visiting French politician a platform to express support for same-sex marriage.

The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Senegal listed pre-electoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human rights problems.

A campaign to raise the maximum penalty to 15 years has run since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pressing for the increase as of July 2024. The 15-year figure was not enacted; the 2026 amendment sets the range at five to ten years.
tangentialFactors:
Senegal refused recommendations made at the Universal Periodic Review in October 2009 and again in October 2013 to amend or repeal legislation punishing conduct on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, to establish a moratorium on Article 319, to ensure non-discrimination, protection and integration, and to criminalise orientation-based violence. The refusal was reasoned on the basis that being homosexual is not a crime although same-sex acts are.

On 6 February 2009 the president authorised a man to change his name to a woman's name in order to emphasise his feminine side, an act reported at the time as causing no controversy. It is a single documented administrative instance of a name change reflecting feminine presentation and does not amount to a legal gender recognition procedure.

The 2008 Dakar prosecution ended in acquittal on appeal in April 2009, so convictions under Article 319 are not final at first instance. The men had by then spent months in custody and been tortured, and the reversal did not alter the statute.

The demand for a 15-year maximum, pressed since 2020, was overtaken by the 2026 amendment, which sets five to ten years rather than the 15 years the campaign sought.
localsOnly:
Residents have no general anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only related statutory limits concern revealing or stigmatising depiction of sexual orientation, which regulate expression rather than protect against discrimination in employment, housing, health care or services.

Local LGBT organisations operate at an exceedingly low profile because of the criminal provisions and social stigma, and Senegalese media rarely report hatred or violence against LGBT people. Incidents therefore tend to surface through family or neighbourhood action rather than through official reporting.

Detention conditions carry specific risk. Police have arrested people on second-hand reports alone, and detainees have been mistreated in custody because of their sexual orientation. In the 2008 case the accused were held segregated from other inmates because those inmates threatened them, and they were tortured repeatedly while in police custody.

Violence within families and communities is documented. A gay male couple near Dakar were beaten by a parent in December 2012 after being caught having sex. In mid-2009 the bodies of people locally described as goor-gigen, man-woman, were dug up from cemeteries, including the May 2009 case in Thies where a corpse was disinterred twice, left beside the grave and then dumped outside the family home after reburial.
outOfScopeNotes:
The February 2026 arrest figures are not reconciled: one source reports 22 men arrested within two weeks, another reports 17 arrests for "acts against nature" in early February. Whether these describe the same operation is unresolved.

The report that 71 of the 99 men arrested in August face up to 20 years is not reconciled with the five-to-ten-year range set by the 2026 amendment. The source does not explain the doubling, and the year of that round-up is not stated.

The scope of the penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith is not defined in the available sources, and it is not sourced whether it has been applied.

Whether the 2026 amendment is in force and how it is being applied to foreign visitors is not sourced. The status of the 15-year proposal after July 2024 is likewise not sourced beyond the enactment of the five-to-ten-year range.

No information was located on how the promotion and support ban is applied to non-citizens, on entry screening practice at ports of entry, or on how border officers handle travellers whose document markers differ from their presentation. The only border incident in the inventory is the 20 February 2026 detention of a man attempting to leave the country.
